docs.title: Home
docs.text: MicroDict is an advanced dictionary lookup program: it is the dictionary program it descends from, with the web engine taken out — articles are rendered by Qt's own rich-text engine, so the program needs no Chromium, no network stack and no bundled fonts.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• Supports many dictionary formats, such as MDX, DSL, StarDict, XDXF, Slob, DictD, BGL, GLS, Aard, SDictionary — see dictionary formats
  • Supports special types of "dictionaries", such as external programs, morphology, transliteration and audio files — see sources management
  • Built-in full-text search
  • Supports user-submitted pronunciation recordings
  • One look only: no style sheets, no themes, no font overrides — see appearance
  • Follows the desktop's colours and its dark/light choice, including the accent colour, and switches together with the desktop without a restart
  • On Linux: one fully static binary for x86-64 and aarch64 — no shared libraries, no interpreter, no bundled fonts (how it is built)

The full dependency ledger is in DEPENDENCIES.md; what the article view can and cannot render is in Article rendering.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
Start the program and type a word into the search box. To have dictionaries found, add their folders under Edit → Dictionaries → Files; see managing sources.

Install covers the Linux AppImage — x86_64 and aarch64 — and building from source. macOS is source-only, and there is no Windows build.

docs.title: Index file
docs.text:
Each index file has 4 sections.

  1. IdxHeader:
  2. ExtraInfo (Being used but unnamed in source code):
  3. Chunks:
  4. BtreeIndex:

The IdxHeader are 32bits blocks of various meta info of the index. The most important info are chunksOffset and indexRootOffset pointing to the starting offset of BtreeIndex and Chunks.

Some dicts only have one ExtraInfo: the dictionaryName which is an uint32 size of a string followed and the string.

Each chunk contains uint32 size of uncompressed data, uint32 size of zlib compressed data, and the zlib compressed data.

The Chunks maybe used by both IdxHeader and BtreeIndex.

By adding new a new chunk to Chunks and store an offset to IdxHeader, ExtraInfo can store arbitrary long information.

BtreeIndex is a zlib compressed typical btree implementation in which each Node will include word info and a offset that pointing to corresponding chunk's position.

Note that a chunk only includes necessary data to find an article, and it does not contain the word.

The exact data in chunk is decided and interpreted by dictionary implementations. For example, the starting and ending position of an article in a dictionary file.

docs.title: What's under the hood after a word is queried?
docs.text:
After typing a word into the search box and pressing enter, the article view is asked to show gdlookup://localhost?word=<wanted word>. There is no browser and no URL-scheme handler: ArticleView recognises that address itself and asks ArticleMaker for the page, which starts the DataRequests on the dictionary formats. Resource files are requested through bres:// and resolved the same way, in-process - a static binary cannot dlopen() anything, and there is no network request left to intercept.

The HTML that comes back is then handed to QTextBrowser, which is a much smaller capability set than a web engine's: see Article rendering for what that means in practice.

docs.title: Article rendering
docs.text: MicroDict renders dictionary articles with Qt's rich-text engine (QTextBrowser / QTextDocument), not with a browser. Everything else on this page follows from that one choice.

docs.title: Why this engine
docs.text: A browser engine would pull in QtWebEngine, QtWebChannel, a sandbox helper, a separate render process and a network stack — none of which can be linked statically on musl. Without them there is one static binary. What QTextDocument does not have is JavaScript and modern CSS layout.

docs.title: The adapter
docs.text:
ArticleMaker still produces the same web pages it always did. Before QTextDocument sees them, src/lite/lite_html.cc rewrites them so that what is left is renderable and means the same thing:

  • Unknown tags are mapped, not dropped. <article>, <section>, <header>, <footer>, <nav>, <aside>, <figure>, <main> become <div>; <mark>, <abbr>, <small>, <time>, <label> become <span>; <kbd>/<samp> become <code>. The paragraph structure the article stylesheet depends on survives.
  • Subtrees that cannot render are removed with their content: script, noscript, form, button, select, textarea, object, video, audio, canvas, inline svg, math, template, dialog, iframe. Deleting them is deliberate: leaving them in would show their source text.
  • display: none is honoured by deleting the element. The rich-text engine ignores that property, so every element MicroDict's own stylesheet hides — gdfromprefix, gddicticon, collapse_expand_area, bglpos, MediaWiki's mw-editsection and friends — is removed instead.
  • Collapsed articles and DSL optional parts are expanded. Without JavaScript there is no way to expand them later, so they are shown from the start. Preferences → Advanced → "Expand optional parts" still controls .dsl_opt.
  • <style> contents are sanitized. Qt's CSS parser has no at-rules, so @media / @supports / @layer / @container / @scope blocks are unwrapped (their rules are kept unconditionally) and @import / @font-face are dropped.
  • Scripts cannot be reached. Every on*="…" attribute is removed and javascript: URLs and bare # hrefs are neutralised.
  • <title> is taken out of the body and used as the tab title.

docs.title: What CSS is honoured
docs.text:
Qt implements a documented subset of HTML and CSS — see Qt's Rich Text HTML Subset and Rich Text CSS Subset pages for the authoritative list. In practice, inside dictionary articles:

  • Works: element, class and id selectors; color, background-color, font-family, font-size in absolute units, font-weight, font-style, text-align, text-indent, text-decoration, vertical-align, margin, white-space: pre, list-style-type, tables with border, colspan, rowspan, scope.
  • Does not work: flexbox, grid, position: fixed/absolute/sticky, display: none (handled by the adapter instead), ::before/::after generated content, CSS custom properties and var(), transforms, transitions, animations, float around images in the way a browser does it, overflow, padding, border on anything but a <table>, border-radius, outline, box-shadow, opacity, font-size in em or %, background-image, media queries (unwrapped, so their rules always apply).

A dictionary whose layout depends on the second list degrades to plain document flow: the text is still there and still readable, the columns and boxes are not.

docs.title: Colours and dark mode
docs.text:
The desktop's palette is applied to the whole interface and then written into the article as a <style> block. It is the only source of colour in the page: before any article style sheet is handed to the engine, lite_html.cc strips every colour declaration out of it. That is not caution for its own sake — the engine lets a sheet containing a construct it does not understand win over a later sheet regardless of order, so "put the palette last" does not reliably work. One a:hover rule in one sheet was enough to make that sheet's background: white beat the palette block.

What is left is structure: the built-in src/stylesheets/article-style.css says which elements are blocks, which are bold and how far they are indented, and nothing about colour. A dictionary's own explicit colours are content and are left alone — an XDXF <c c="red"> still renders red.

There is no Dark Reader — that was a JavaScript script — so dark mode is exactly "the desktop's colours, applied to the page". Change the desktop's colour scheme and the article changes with it, no restart needed. There is nothing to override on top of that — see Appearance.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text: The program ships no font files and names none of its own: articles ask for the generic CSS families (serif, sans-serif, monospace) and the host's fontconfig answers with the machine's faces. There is no font preference — the four generic families are mapped onto the engine's own defaults and that is the end of it.

docs.title: Images
docs.text: Article resources (bres://) are resolved in-process — there is no network request and no plugin directory. SVG files work because the qsvg image-format plugin is compiled into the binary. An inline <svg> element in article markup is dropped (the engine cannot draw it); <img src="…svg"> is fine. Images that arrive after the document was built are filled into it as they load.

docs.title: Navigation, search, audio
docs.text:
• gdlookup://, bword://, gdfrom://, bres:// and friends are recognised by the view itself; there is no URL-scheme handler and no interceptor.
  • Jumping between articles and to a dictionary's head is done with the document's own anchors (gdfrom-…), not with scripts.
  • In-page search (Ctrl+F) and the full-text search panel's "highlight all" use the engine's selection highlighting; there is no mark.js.
  • Audio playback is unaffected: it never went through the article view (audio engine).

docs.title: What stops working
docs.text:
• Anything a dictionary's JavaScript does: popups, tabs inside an article, collapsible widgets, search boxes in the article.
  • MathJax/TeX in slob dictionaries — MathJax is JavaScript, so formulas stay as their source text.
  • Websites and iframes: there is nothing to load them with (dictionary formats).
  • Articles laid out with flexbox/grid/absolute positioning.

If a specific dictionary renders badly, compare it with upstream and say so in the issue tracker — the adapter is deliberately small, and a missing tag mapping or a class that should be deleted is an easy fix.

docs.title: Command Line Interface
docs.text:
MicroDict's command line is the one it was forked with, minus the options that belonged to removed features taken out. The executable is microdict.

microdict [options] [word]

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
Option Description -h, --help Show the built-in help -v, --version Print the version and diagnostic information -l, --log-to-file Save debug messages to microdict_log.txt in the configuration folder -g, --group-name <name> Switch the main window to the named dictionary group -r, --reset-window-state Forget the saved window geometry and state word Word or phrase to look up at startup

microdict --help is always the current truth; this page is not.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
microdict hello                       # look a word up in the main window
microdict -r                          # start with a clean window state
microdict -l                          # write microdict_log.txt into the config folder
microdict -v                          # version + build diagnostics

docs.title: URL scheme
docs.text:
The desktop entry registers the program as the handler for microdict: and dict: URLs:

microdict://<word>

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text: Variable Effect MICRODICT_FORCE_WAYLAND Force the native Wayland platform MICRODICT_FORCE_XCB Force the X11 platform. Only meaningful in a build that contains the xcb plugin — the static Linux binary ships the Wayland and offscreen plugins and nothing else QT_QPA_PLATFORM Qt's own override; offscreen is what the repository's headless checks use and it wins over both variables above

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: • MicroDict is single-instance: if it is already running, the arguments are handed to the running copy through its local peer (MicroDict) and the second process exits. That peer name is this program's own: QtLocalPeer keeps six letters of it as the instance id, so another program running at the same time keeps its own.

docs.title: Custom dictionary
docs.text:
A metadata.toml, which uses toml format, can be used to customize or override some properties of a certain dictionary. It is also used in auto grouping by metadata

The metadata.toml should be placed on each dictionary's root folder (beside dictionary files) like

.
├── Cambridge
│    ├── metadata.toml < here
│    ├── Cambridge.idx
│    ├── Cambridge.info
│    ├── Cambridge.syn
│    └── Cambridge.dict.dz
└── Collins
     ├── metadata.toml < here
     ├── res.zip
     └── Collins.dsl

docs.title: Override display name
docs.text:
Some dictionary formats' display is embedded inside the dictionary, which cannot be easily changed, but you can add the following to override it.

[metadata]
name = "New Name"

This New Name will be appeared as the dictionary name.

docs.title: Disable full-text search
docs.text:
fts=false

[metadata]
name="New Name"

The fts field's value can be on/off, 1/0 ,true/false etc.

fts=false

will disable the current dictionary's full-text search.

You can check the full-text search status on each dictionary's info dialog.

Note that it is possible to enable full text for a single dictionary by disabling full-text search in the Preferences dialog, and set fts=true for that dictionary.

docs.title: Developer
docs.text:
If you know some C++ and optionally some Qt, you can start to modify MicroDict right now.

This page is a brief introduction on how to get started.

For technical details see how to build from source and, for the release build, Build the static Linux binary. The dependency ledger — what is linked, what was dropped and why — is DEPENDENCIES.md in the repository root.

docs.title: Install Qt
docs.text:
To install Qt on macOS, use the Qt Online Installer. It can be downloaded from Qt for Open Source. On Linux, install your distribution's Qt 6 development packages — see how to build from source for the list.

Those Qt components are needed:

  • Qt
    • 6.12 (Or another version)
      • Qt5 Compatible Module
      • Multimedia
      • SVG
      • Tools (for lrelease)
      • Wayland (Linux only — the platform plugin and the D-Bus portal client)
    • Qt Creator (optional)
      • CMake
      • Ninja

Not needed at all: Qt WebEngine, Qt WebChannel and Qt TextToSpeech.

CMake and Ninja are needed.

docs.title: Install a compiler
docs.text: On Linux, Alpine's build-base (GCC 15 in this fork's image); any C++23 compiler works. For macOS, install XCode.

docs.title: Obtain dependencies
docs.text:
On Linux they come from the distribution — except Xapian, which must be the 1.4 series, and the libraries the static image builds from source.

For macOS, install Homebrew and install the packages the build looks for: cmake/Deps_macOS.cmake lists every library name pkg_check_modules resolves, and how to build from source gives the brew install spelling.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
First, get MicroDict's source code by Cloning a repository.

Then choose your favorite IDE/editor and load the CMakeLists.txt. If unsure, just use Qt Creator.

docs.title: Qt Creator
docs.text:
Open CMakeLists.txt from Qt Creator, then you wil choose a "Kit" which is pretty much a Qt installation.

Qt Creator usually can auto-detect your Qt installation. In case it doesn't, check out "Kit" settings.

By default everything is built; the only switch left is WITH_QT_MULTIMEDIA, the one internal audio player. Upstream's WITH_EPWING_SUPPORT, WITH_ZIM, WITH_TTS, WITH_X11, WITH_FFMPEG_PLAYER and USE_ALTERNATIVE_NAME do not exist here.

Then, hit the "Run" button at bottom-right corner should build and run MicroDict.

docs.title: Command Line only
docs.text:
See how to build from source.

Qt's doc: Building projects on the command line

docs.title: Visual Studio Code
docs.text:
Install CMake Tools.

Then open MicroDict's folder, and the CMake extension will kicks in.

Then add Qt's path and various other options to configure arguments.

-DCMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<your Qt install path>

docs.title: Related Things
docs.text:
Please follow C++ Core Guidelines and write modern C++ code.

Qt's documentation

docs.title: Dictionary formats
docs.text: Popular dictionary formats are all supported.

docs.title: Local Dictionaries Sources
docs.text:
• MDict dictionaries (.mdx/.mdd)
  • StarDict dictionaries (.ifo/.dict./.idx/.syn)
  • DSL dictionaries (ABBYY Lingvo source files .dsl(.dz))
  • XDXF dictionaries (.xdxf(.dz))
  • Slob (Aard 2) dictionaries (.slob)
  • DictD dictionaries (.index/.dict(.dz))
  • Aard Dictionary dictionaries, outdated predecessor of Slob (.aar)
  • SDictionary dictionaries (.dct)
  • Babylon glossary builder source files (.gls(.dz))
  • Babylon dictionaries, complete support with images and resources (.BGL)

  • ABBYY Lingvo sound archives (.lsa/.dat)

  • Sound files in separate folders. File names are used as word

  • Zipped sound pack. Sound files zipped, but with extension changed from .zip to (.zips)

docs.title: Network Sources
docs.text: None. MicroDict is built without a network stack: there is no DICT protocol client, no Wikipedia/Wiktionary, no LinguaLibre/Forvo pronunciations and no "any site whose address line can carry the word" source. Dictionary files are read from disk only.

docs.title: Other Sources
docs.text: Various special "dictionaries" can be added, such as Programs, Morphology and Transliteration. Their doc is at Sources Management.

docs.title: Converting between formats
docs.text:
MicroDict does not provide any dictionary modification functionality.

To convert between formats, try tools like pyglossary.

docs.title: Custom Dictionary Icon
docs.text:
Every local dictionary can have a custom icon. Supported formats are PNG, JPEG, GIF, SVG, WebP, ICO and BMP.

For most dictionary formats, a dictionary's icon file should have the same basename as the main dictionary file and be placed beside the main dictionary file. For example:

.
├── My_best_dictionary.mdx <- the main dictionary file
└── My_best_dictionary.svg <- the icon

For XDXF, MicroDict will prioritize to use icon16.png, icon32.png or dict.bmp in the dictionary folder as icon.

docs.title: Stardict
docs.text:
Main file of Stardict dictionary (.dict) can be compressed by Dictzip program to reduce its size.

Resource storage folder (images, style sheets, etc.) should be named as res beside other dictionary files.

The res folder can be compressed into res.zip or my_name.res.zip (for main dict filename my_name.ifo/dict). This zip file should also be placed beside other dictionary files. The internal structure of the zip file should not have a top level folder.

docs.title: ABBYY Lingvo (.dsl)
docs.text:
Main file of ABBYY Lingvo dictionary (.dsl) can be compressed by Dictzip program to reduce its size.

Additional dictionary resources (images, sound files, etc.) also can be compressed into zip archive. This archive must be named on main dictionary file name (include extension) with adding ".files.zip" and placed beside other dictionary files. If main file of your dictionary, for example, named "My_best_dictionary.dsl" therefore archive with resources must be named "My_best_dictionary.dsl.files.zip".

MicroDict supports the "#SOUND_DICTIONARY" directive. Sounds missing in the resources of the dictionary will be searched first in the dictionary specified in this directive.

docs.title: DictD and XDXF compression
docs.text: Main file of DictD dictionary (.dict) or XDXF dictionary (.xdxf) can be compressed into *.dict.dz or *.xdxf.dz by Dictzip program to reduce its size.

docs.title: Slob
docs.text: A slob dictionary that bundles MathJax cannot have its TeX formulas rendered here: MathJax is JavaScript and there is no JavaScript engine. The formulas appear as their source text.

docs.title: GLS
docs.text: Main file of Babylon source dictionary must be in UTF-8 (or UTF-16 with BOM) encoding. It can be compressed by Dictzip program to reduce its size. MicroDict reads from the dictionary header the "### Glossary title:", "### Author:", "### Description:", "### Source language:" and "### Target language:" fields only. Dictionary header must be concluded with "### Glossary section:" mark.

docs.title: ABBYY Lingvo sound archives
docs.text: ABBYY Lingvo sound archives are set of sound files packed into one file of some specific format. These files can be called directly from matches list or from dictionary articles.

docs.title: Sound files in separate folders
docs.text: The separate folder with sound files can be added into MicroDict dictionaries list. MicroDict will handle this folders like ABBYY Lingvo sound archives (inapplicable in portable mode).

docs.title: Zips sound packs
docs.text: Zips sound pack is zip archive with extension ".zips" contains set of sound files. To create suck pack it needs to compress sound files into zip archive and change extension of this archive to ".zips". MicroDict will handle such sound packs like ABBYY Lingvo sound archives.

docs.title: General notes
docs.text: At every launch MicroDict scan folders with dictionaries to create dictionaries list. The more files in these folder is the more time for scanning. Therefore it is recommended to compress dictionary resources into zip archives and to use Zips sound packs instead of sound files in separate folders.

docs.title: Bugs Reporting
docs.text:
Report any bugs and dysfunctions to issues

If a certain dictionary leads to problems, you must attach the dict files or provide download links in bug reports.

Attach your version info from the menu "About" --> "Copy version info".

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
The quickest thing to attach to a report is the program's own log.

Start MicroDict from a terminal and keep the output, or start it with the command line flag --log-to-file; that writes microdict_log.txt into the configuration folder the next time the program runs.

docs.title: macOS Tips
docs.text:
macOS has a built-in crash reporter. Copy all the info from the bug report window.

Try to start the program from the command line and save the logs, as above.

docs.title: Linux Tips
docs.text:
If you have no clue, search and learn how to obtain coredumps using tools provided by your distro, and/or learn how to use a debugger. Now is the time.

Noticeably, in recent years, popular distros support new technologies such as systemd-coredump and Debuginfod. Traditional approaches include installing debug packages or building from source.

At least, you should start the program in the terminal and upload the log.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: MicroDict is not in any distribution's package repositories and not on Flathub, which carries upstream's program instead. The fork also installs nothing itself — there are no .deb/.rpm packages, no Flatpak, no cmake --install rules on Linux and no AppStream metadata. For Linux there is exactly one kind of artifact, and it is a single file: an AppImage, published for x86_64 and aarch64.

docs.title: Linux: the AppImage
docs.text:
The releases page carries one file per architecture plus their checksums:

MicroDict-<version>-x86_64.AppImage
MicroDict-<version>-aarch64.AppImage
SHA256SUMS.txt

sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS.txt
chmod +x MicroDict-<version>-<arch>.AppImage
./MicroDict-<version>-<arch>.AppImage

That is the whole installation. An AppImage is a filesystem image with a small runtime in front of it: it mounts itself (or unpacks to a temporary directory when FUSE is unavailable) and starts the program inside. Nothing is written outside the program's own config directories, and removing the program means deleting the file.

What is inside it is the fork's fully static binary — 0 NEEDED entries, no PT_INTERP — together with the three things a bare binary cannot carry: the translations, the icon and the desktop entry. So the file also behaves like a normal desktop program: it has an icon, an integration tool can put it in a menu, and its .desktop entry is what the "start on login" preference copies into the autostart directory the desktop reads — $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/autostart/, which is ~/.config/autostart/ unless the user moved it. The copy rewrites Exec= to the AppImage itself, because the path inside a mounted image disappears once it exits. A writable directory named MicroDict-<version>-<arch>.AppImage.config next to the file makes the program keep its configuration there instead of in ~/.config/microdict; the login entry still goes to ~/.config/autostart/, because no desktop ever looks inside that directory — see Portable mode.

The requirements are the ones the binary has anyway:

  • x86-64 or aarch64 Linux. Both the payload and the runtime in front of it are built for one of the two; the file name's suffix is what uname -m prints.
  • Wayland. The static build contains the wayland and offscreen platform plugins and nothing else — no XCB plugin, so there is no X11 session to fall back to. Under X11, run it through a Wayland compositor (cage, weston --backend=x11). See Wayland.
  • Fonts and a portal come from the host. The program ships no fonts and names none of its own: articles ask for the generic CSS families and the host's fontconfig answers with the machine's faces. Global hotkeys and the desktop's light/dark choice are asked of xdg-desktop-portal; without a portal, hotkeys are simply not registered.

One thing you may notice on the console and can ignore:

qt.qpa.services: Failed to register with host portal: Could not register app ID:
App info not found for 'io.github.dsvi.microdict'

Qt's Wayland platform asks the portal to look the desktop entry up, and the portal — a separate process — searches its own data directories, where an entry that lives inside an AppImage is not. Nothing depends on that registration here; it is the sound of the program not being installed anywhere, which is the point.

docs.title: The bare binary
docs.text:
The binary is not published on its own: the AppImage is the only release artifact. To get the bare executable, build it:

git clone https://github.com/dsvi/MicroDict
cd MicroDict
./packaging/docker/build.sh          # needs Docker; ~30 min from scratch

It lands in ./build-out/microdict, with its translations linked into it. Everything the AppImage wraps around the binary is optional; the binary runs alone. ./build-appimage.sh is the shorter path: it stops after the packaging stage and writes just build-out/MicroDict-<version>-<arch>.AppImage.

./user-install.sh builds it and installs the rest around it: the binary into $XDG_BIN_HOME or ~/.local/bin, the icon and a .desktop entry under ~/.local/share. That entry is what makes the installed copy behave like a normal desktop program — right-clicking it offers the two delete actions, and it is what the "start on login" preference copies into the autostart directory.

Docker is only the build farm. docker run of the built image works too, but then the container — not the host — decides which fonts exist:

docker build -f packaging/docker/Dockerfile -t microdict-static .
docker run --rm -e XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/cfg -v $PWD/cfg:/cfg -v $PWD/dicts:/dicts \
    -v /usr/share/fonts:/usr/share/fonts:ro --device /dev/shm microdict-static <word>

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
There are no pre-built macOS binaries: the workflow that published them was removed when the release automation was reduced to the AppImage. Build it yourself — Build from source, whose macOS section covers macdeployqt and code signing. There the install tree is the deliverable, so cmake --install produces MicroDict.app, and a .dmg too once create-dmg is installed.

There is no Windows build: the tree has no Windows dependency file, no Windows packaging and no CI for it.

docs.title: From source, on any system
docs.text: See Build from source. The Linux section there is the plain dynamic build; the static one is Build the static Linux binary. Neither installs anything on Linux: the program finds its data relative to its own executable.

docs.title: Version policy
docs.text: The fork keeps its own number, in the VERSION file at the root of the repository. That file is the only place the number is written: CMake reads it into PROJECT_VERSION, the About dialog and the PROGRAM_VERSION compile definition take it from there, and the AppImage file name is built from it. It says nothing about which upstream commit the tree last merged.

docs.title: Managing groups
docs.text:
At Edit -> Dictionaries -> Groups, you can create and edit dictionary groups.

To add a dictionary into a group, just drag it from the dictionary list into the group window on the right. To remove a dict, just drag it back to the dictionary list. Hold Shift to select a range of dictionaries or hold Ctrl to select multiple dictionaries.

Additionally, multiple strategies of automatic grouping are provided:

  • based on the language info embedded within dictionary files
  • based on the folder structure
  • based on customizable metadata files

docs.title: Auto groups by dictionary language
docs.text:
For formats like DSL, which has embedded language from / to metadata, MicroDict will use the dictionary's built-in metadata.

For other formats, MicroDict will try finding the last {id}-{id} pair delimited by non-alphabets in dictionary name or main file name to extract languages. The {id} is 2 or 3 letters ISO 639 codes. For example, if a dictionary named some name en-zh, it will be automatically grouped into en-zh.

Groups created in this method also include a context menu when right-click the group name, in which you can do additional dictionaries grouping by source or target language and combine dictionaries in more large groups.

docs.title: Auto groups by folders
docs.text:
Click the "Group by folders" will group your dicts based on folder structure.

Two dictionaries will be in the same group if their container folder's direct parent is the same.

For example, the structure below will be auto grouped into two groups:

  • English<>Chinese with Cambridge, Collins and Oxford
  • English<>Russian with dictA, dictB, Wikipedia_ru and Wikipedia
.
├── English<>Chinese
│   ├── Cambridge
│   │   ├── Cambridge.dict.dz
│   │   ├── Cambridge.idx
│   │   ├── Cambridge.info
│   │   └── Cambridge.syn
│   ├── Collins
│   │   ├── Collins.dsl
│   │   └── res.zip
│   └── Oxford
│       ├── Oxford.css
│       ├── Oxford.mdd
│       └── Oxford.mdx
└── English<>Russian
    ├── dsl
    │   ├── dictA.dsl
    │   └── dictB.dsl
    └── slob
        ├── Wikipedia_ru.slob
        └── Wikipedia_en.slob

Note that if two groups share the same name but in different folder, then upper level's folder name will be prepended with group name. The Example below will be grouped into epistularum/Japanese and Mastameta/Japanese.

More levels of folder nesting are not supported.

.
├─epistularum
│   └─Japanese   <- Group
│       └─DictA  <- Dict Files's container folder
│           └─ DictA Files
├─Mastameta
│   └─Japanese   <- Group
│       └─DictB  <- Dict Files's container folder
│           └─ DictB Files

docs.title: Auto groups by metadata.toml
docs.text:
Click the "group by metadata" will group your dicts based on metadata.toml.

The metadata.toml should be placed beside dictionary files. One metadata.toml for each dictionary.

The metadata file uses TOML format.

categories = [ "English", "Russian", "Chinese" ]

# the following `langfrom` , `langto` fields have not been supported yet.
[metadata]
name = "New Name"
langfrom = "English"
langto = "Russian"

For example,

.
├── Cambridge
│    ├── metadata.toml     (A)
│    ├── Cambridge.idx
│    ├── Cambridge.info
│    ├── Cambridge.syn
│    └── Cambridge.dict.dz
└── Collins
     ├── metadata.toml
     ├── res.zip
     └── Collins.dsl       (B)

The content of the metadata (A) is 

categories = ["en-zh", "汉英词典"]

The content of the metadata (B) is 

categories = ["图片词典", "en-zh", "汉英词典"]

The structure above will be auto grouped into three groups:

  • en-zh with Cambridge, Collins
  • 图片词典 with Collins
  • 汉英词典 with Cambridge,Collins

Note: Dictionaries without metadata.toml won't be auto-grouped.

docs.title: Managing dictionary sources
docs.text:
Dictionary management dialog can be opened via menu Edit -> Dictionaries.

To use local dictionaries, add them via Sources -> Files.

To inspect or disable individual dictionaries, go Edit -> Dictionaries -> Dictionaries.

If you have too many dictionaries, consider using Groups to manage them.

docs.title: Files
docs.text:
Here you can add local dictionaries.

Press the "Add" button and select folders that include your local dictionaries. To search every subfolder, enable the "Recursive":

MicroDict will scan these folders and add found dictionaries to the dictionaries list.

The "Rescan" button starts a forced scan of all folders in the list.

docs.title: Sound Dirs
docs.text:
Similar to Files, you can either add a folder which contains sound files or a .zip archive which contains the sound files.

MicroDict will search through the sound file names when querying words.

docs.title: Morphology
docs.text:
A word could have several forms, but sometimes a dictionary only contains one form that could not be found unless you search the normalized form.

Morphology dictionary uses Hunspell's morphological analysis to obtain word's variant forms.

You can specify a path that includes Hunspell format data files (.aff + .dic). MicroDict will scan this folder and create a list of available dictionaries.

One possible source of Hunspell dictionaries is LibreOffice's dictionaries.

The detailed document about the affix file (.aff) and the dict file (.dic) can be found at hunspell.5.

Note that lots of Hunspell's dictionaries are for mostly for spell checking, and they may lack special morphological rules (For example, related words don't share the same stem in .dic file). There are some specially tailored hunspell dicts to use for Morphology. Such as

  • https://github.com/Ajatt-Tools/hunspell-ja

docs.title: Programs
docs.text:
Here you can add external applications. To add such an application, you should set the command line for its launch, name for the dictionary list and application type.

The %GDWORD% in command line will be replaced by word from search line.

Program type Purpose Audio Play sound. Text Text printed by the program will be shown as separate article. HTML HTML printed by the program will be shown as separate article. Prefix match A list of words printed by the program will be added to search bar's completion list.

Other than "Audio", the program should print the content to standard output.

In the "Icon" column, you can set a custom icon for every application. If you add icon file name without a path, MicroDict will search this file in the configuration folder.

Note

The word will be written to stdin in UTF-8 if the command line doesn't contain %GDWORD%.

For Python3.6+, reading stdin as UTF-8 is the default behaviour. For older versions, you may need to change PYTHONIOENCODING.

For Node.js, try process.stdin.setEncoding('utf8');.

If you cannot change how your language handles stdin's encoding, try store the data read from the stdin as bytes and call related methods that interpret bytes as UTF-8 strings.

docs.title: Transliteration
docs.text: Here you can add transliteration algorithms. To add an algorithm to the dictionaries list, just set a mark beside it. When such a dictionary is added to the current dictionaries group, MicroDict will search for the word in the input line as well as the result of its handling by the corresponding transliteration algorithm.

docs.title: Chinese and Japanese character conversion
docs.text:
MicroDict ships with a built-in conversion

Option Effect Simplified (Mainland) Traditional Chinese and Japanese Shinjitai input is also searched as simplified Chinese. Traditional (Taiwan/Standard) Simplified Chinese and Japanese Shinjitai input is also searched as traditional Chinese (Taiwan standard). Hong Kong variant Simplified Chinese and Japanese Shinjitai input is also searched as traditional Chinese (Hong Kong variant). Japanese Shinjitai Simplified and traditional Chinese input is also searched as Japanese Shinjitai.

Every ticked option is registered as a separate dictionary in the list below, so it can be enabled per dictionary group. The word can be typed in any of the variants and still match the entries, for example searching 図書館 also finds 圖書館 and 图书馆.

The conversion data is provided by OpenCC; see Customize the opencc for the configuration files in use. If you want to define your own transliteration rules, see Custom transliteration.

docs.title: What is not here
docs.text: Upstream's Websites, DICT servers and System Text-to-speech engines tabs are gone: they needed the network stack or the web engine. A website dictionary can still be approximated with a Programs entry that fetches the page itself and prints HTML, but nothing in this fork runs the page's scripts — see Article rendering.

docs.title: Configuration folders
docs.text: MicroDict keeps its own files everywhere. It can be installed next to the program it was forked from, and neither one touches the other's files.

docs.title: Where this fork keeps things
docs.text:
What Linux / BSD macOS Configuration, history, favourites $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/microdict (default ~/.config/microdict) ~/.microdict Data (dictionaries' extra files) $XDG_DATA_HOME/microdict (default ~/.local/share/microdict) — Search indexes $XDG_CACHE_HOME/microdict/index (default ~/.cache/microdict/index) — Read-only program data (OpenCC data) beside the executable: <binary dir>/../share/microdict inside the .app Translations inside the executable — they are linked in as a Qt resource inside the executable

Nothing is installed to $PREFIX on Linux, so that path is worked out from where the program was started from rather than compiled in: the AppImage keeps its payload at usr/bin and usr/share/microdict inside the mounted image, and a bare binary with no such directory beside it simply has no OpenCC data. The translations take no part in that search — they are linked into the executable.

XDG_CONFIG_HOME &co. are honoured, so a container or a test run can point the whole program at a scratch directory:

XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/tmp/cfg XDG_DATA_HOME=/tmp/data XDG_CACHE_HOME=/tmp/cache \
    microdict

docs.title: Nothing is read from the old program's folders
docs.text:
The fork reads and writes only directories named microdict. Upstream fell back to a directory named after itself whenever the XDG variables were unset, and an older revision of this fork copied upstream's config into its own directory on the first run. Neither happens now: starting this program beside upstream changes nothing over there, and the fork's own config is the only configuration file it will ever open.

To bring settings across from the old program, copy its config file into $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/microdict/config yourself.

Absolute dictionary paths carry over as they are; relative ones were relative to the old config directory, so adjust them under Edit → Dictionaries → Files. Keys belonging to features this fork does not have — Anki, printing, text to speech, ZIM, web sites — are ignored on the way in and are gone the next time the file is written. Search indexes are not in that file at all; they are rebuilt in the fork's own cache directory.

docs.title: If the configuration is broken
docs.text:
A config file that cannot be parsed does not get silently overwritten. The program asks what to do; choosing to continue with default settings renames the file to

config.<yyyyMMdd_HHmmss>.bad

and starts over. Choosing not to continue leaves the file exactly where it was.

docs.title: Portable mode
docs.text: A portable folder next to the executable moves everything into <exe directory>/portable: no XDG, no registry. See Portable mode.

docs.title: Single instance
docs.text: The program refuses to start twice; the second invocation hands its command line to the running one. The IPC name it registers is MicroDict. QtLocalPeer keeps only the first six letters of a peer name, so this one registers MicroD; upstream's peer keeps its own name and the two programs can run at the same time.

docs.title: Verifying it
docs.text:
The repository ships a script that checks exactly the behaviour above — the microdict directories created and used, nothing at all created anywhere else, the fork's own config the only one there is, and a truncated one left whole rather than rewritten:

QT_QPA_PLATFORM=offscreen sh packaging/docker/migtest.sh

It prints === migtest.sh: config-directory checks passed === and exits 0 when everything holds.

docs.title: Move the index folder
docs.text:
The index folder stores the full-text search indexes produced by MicroDict. For large dictionaries (e.g. Wikipedia, Wiktionary), the size of these indexes can grow very large, potentially filling up your system drive.

There are generally two approaches to deal with the growing index size:

  • Enable Portable Mode so that indexes are kept in a location of your choosing.
  • Move the index folder in place using a symbolic (soft) link, keeping the original path intact.

This page explains the latter approach.

Note

By default MicroDict keeps its configurations and indexes in the user's home directory. To find out the exact location used on your system, see the storage layout in Portable Mode.

Note

This fork always uses the XDG cache directory for indexes: $XDG_CACHE_HOME/microdict/index, default ~/.cache/microdict/index. Point XDG_CACHE_HOME somewhere else instead of linking if that is simpler — see Configuration folders.

docs.title: Linux, BSD and macOS
docs.text:
1. Close MicroDict.
  2. Copy the index folder to another place, take /mnt/big/index_new for example.
  3. Delete the original index folder.
  4. Create the link:
ln -s /mnt/big/index_new ~/.cache/microdict/index
  1. Run MicroDict.

Warning

Do not put the target folder (e.g. /mnt/big/index_new) inside the folder being linked, otherwise you may create an infinite recursion. Keep them on separate paths.

Warning

Removing the link must not follow it. rm ~/.cache/microdict/index removes the link itself; rm -r on a path with a trailing slash removes the files it points to.

docs.title: Portable Mode
docs.text:
By default, MicroDict keeps its configuration and indexes in the user's XDG directories (see Configuration folders). To keep everything in one portable location, create a portable folder next to the program file; once that folder exists the program launches in portable mode.

Portable Mode is especially convenient when you want to keep all data (including the large full-text search indexes) on an external drive or in a custom folder. If you prefer to keep the existing directory structure and only relocate the growing index folder, see Move the index folder instead.

In portable mode, the configurations and indexes are stored in the portable folder. All dictionaries must be placed in or inside the subfolders of content folder, which located besides the main program file.

Folder structure:

<program directory>/
├── microdict       the program
├── content/              all dictionary files (.mdx, .dsl, .ifo, ...)
│   └── morphology/       morphology dictionaries
└── portable/             everything the program writes lives here
    ├── config            program configuration
    └── index/            full-text search indexes

All dictionary files you want to load can be placed in or inside the subfolders of the content folder described above.

docs.title: Portable mode in an AppImage
docs.text:
The portable folder cannot be used there: everything inside an AppImage is read-only and is gone again when the program exits. The AppImage runtime has its own version of the same idea — a writable directory next to the AppImage file, named after it with .config appended:

/media/usb/MicroDict-0.0.0-x86_64.AppImage
/media/usb/MicroDict-0.0.0-x86_64.AppImage.config/
└── microdict/
    ├── config            program configuration
    └── index/            full-text search indexes

If that directory exists the runtime exports XDG_CONFIG_HOME to it before starting the program, so the configuration — and under it the microdict folder the program uses — is written beside the file rather than in the user's home. A directory with .home appended does the same for $HOME, which moves the data and cache folders along with it. Nothing else changes: dictionaries are still added from wherever they live, since there is no content/ folder inside an image to put them in.

docs.title: Transliteration
docs.text:
Transliteration makes a word findable even when it is written in a different script or character variant. It is configured in the Transliteration tab of the dictionary sources dialog (Edit -> Dictionaries -> Sources).

When such a dictionary is added to the current dictionaries group, MicroDict searches for the word in the input line as well as for the result of its handling by the corresponding transliteration algorithm. Every enabled item is registered as a separate dictionary, so it can also be enabled or disabled per dictionary group.

docs.title: Built-in transliteration
docs.text: Item Description Russian transliteration Converts a word written with the Latin alphabet into Russian, so a Latin transliteration also matches the Cyrillic entries. German transliteration Converts the ae/oe/ue/ss transcription into the German characters ä/ö/ü/ß. Greek transliteration Converts a word written with the Latin alphabet into Greek. Belarusian transliteration Converts a word written with the Latin alphabet into Belarusian. Japanese Romaji Converts Romaji into kana. Hepburn is the supported romanization system, while the Hiragana and Katakana checkboxes select the produced syllabary.

docs.title: Chinese and Japanese character conversion
docs.text:
MicroDict converts the searched word into the ticked character variants, so the word may be typed in any of these variants and still match the entries:

Option Effect Simplified (Mainland) Traditional Chinese and Japanese Shinjitai input is also searched as simplified Chinese. Traditional (Taiwan/Standard) Simplified Chinese and Japanese Shinjitai input is also searched as traditional Chinese (Taiwan standard). Hong Kong variant Simplified Chinese and Japanese Shinjitai input is also searched as traditional Chinese (Hong Kong variant). Japanese Shinjitai Simplified and traditional Chinese input is also searched as Japanese Shinjitai.

For example, searching 図書館 also finds 圖書館 and 图书馆.

The conversion data is provided by OpenCC; see Customize the opencc for the configuration files in use.

docs.title: Custom transliteration
docs.text:
This will enable users to configure their own transliteration if the provided transliteration can not meet the requirements.

The rules only apply to the search phrase. Each line defines one transliteration with the input and the target separated by a semicolon, so a line ae;æ makes MicroDict also search æ when ae is typed.

The rules are entered in the Custom transliteration box on the Transliteration tab of the dictionary sources dialog.

docs.title: Appearance
docs.text: MicroDict has exactly one look, the desktop's. Colours come from the desktop's colour scheme and fonts from the host, and there is no style sheet, no theme picker and no font override — not for dictionary articles and not for its own interface.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text:
The interface is drawn with the desktop's colour scheme and the desktop's font, both chosen by the platform theme. Nothing is read from disk and nothing is picked in Preferences:

  • there is no qt-style.css in the configuration folder, and none is looked for;
  • there is no add-on style folder and no "Add-on style" control;
  • there is no "Interface Style" control — the widget style the platform theme selects is used as it is;
  • there is no "Dark Mode" or "Dark Reader Mode" control: the desktop's colour scheme decides, and a running program follows it as it changes.

docs.title: Article colours
docs.text:
An article's colours are the desktop's colours: the base, the text, the links, the selection and the accent are read from the desktop's colour scheme and written into the page. To change how articles look, change the desktop's colour scheme — the article view follows it immediately, without a restart.

Nothing else sets article colours:

  • Every colour declaration in every article style sheet is removed before the sheet reaches the rendering engine, so the palette block is the only colour source. The built-in src/stylesheets/article-style.css keeps only structure — which elements are blocks, which are bold, how far they are indented.
  • There is no list of article styles to pick from any more, and no article-style.css in the configuration folder is read.
  • A dictionary's own explicit colours are content, not styling, and are left alone: an XDXF <c c="red"> still renders red.

See Article rendering for what the renderer understands.

docs.title: Fonts
docs.text: The program ships no font files and names none of its own. The interface uses the desktop's font. Articles ask for the generic CSS families — serif, sans-serif, monospace — and the host's font configuration resolves them. There is no font preference to set.

docs.title: Accessing the Configuration Folder
docs.text: To access MicroDict's configuration folder, follow these steps based on your operating system:

docs.title: macOS
docs.text: ~/.microdict

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
~/.config/microdict, or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/microdict if that is set.

The fork never uses a configuration directory named after the program it was forked from. See Configuration folders.

docs.title: Configuration File Structure
docs.text:
The configuration folder holds the program's state and nothing style-related:

.
├── config      preferences
├── favorites   saved favorites, written when they change
└── history     search history

There is no style sheet to create here. A qt-style.css or a styles/ folder left over from an older version is simply never opened; both can be deleted.

docs.title: No scripts
docs.text: There is no article-script.js: the article view has no JavaScript engine, so there is nothing to inject into. Restyling, expanding collapsed parts and highlighting are all done by the C++ side (Article rendering).

docs.title: Wayland
docs.text: MicroDict runs as a native Wayland client. The static Linux binary contains the wayland and offscreen Qt platform plugins and nothing else — there is no xcb plugin, so there is no X11 session to fall back to and no XWayland trick that would make one appear.

docs.title: Choosing the platform
docs.text:
Priority at startup:

Setting Effect QT_QPA_PLATFORM honoured first; offscreen is what the repository's headless checks use MICRODICT_FORCE_XCB=1 asks for the X11 platform. Only does anything in a build that actually contains the xcb plugin (a dynamic build on a distribution that ships it); the static binary has no xcb plugin, so the app then simply fails to find a platform MICRODICT_FORCE_WAYLAND=1 force the native Wayland platform nothing set Qt decides, which on a Wayland session means native Wayland 
env MICRODICT_FORCE_WAYLAND=1 microdict

docs.title: How the hotkey and clipboard features reach the desktop
docs.text:
Feature How it works Global hotkey (F12, clipboard lookup) requested from org.freedesktop.portal.GlobalShortcuts; the desktop decides who owns the combination and can refuse it Giving the binding back on exit or when it changes org.kde.kglobalaccel's cleanUp() is called on every component that owns our shortcut id What the lookup reads QClipboard: the clipboard on Wayland, the X11 selection under X11 Position of the main window wherever the compositor puts it; Wayland clients do not position themselves

If xdg-desktop-portal is not running, hotkeys are simply not registered — the program logs that and carries on. Everything else works.

docs.title: Wayland-specific notes
docs.text:
• The window's app_id is io.github.dsvi.microdict, taken from the desktop file the program installs; that is what the taskbar matches the icon against.
  • Fractional scaling and HiDPI are handled by Qt and the compositor; nothing in the program overrides them.
  • Input methods work through Qt 6's Wayland input-method protocol, provided the compositor offers one.
  • Screenshots of the scan popup are the compositor's business; the program never grabs the screen.

docs.title: Running under X11 only
docs.text: There is no supported path in the static binary. Either run a Wayland compositor (weston, cage, or a Wayland session), or build the program yourself: a dynamic build against a distribution Qt that ships the xcb plugin gets the X11 platform back, and MICRODICT_FORCE_XCB=1 then selects it.

docs.title: Audio playback
docs.text:
By default the program plays pronunciations through its own internal player, which is Qt Multimedia — the only internal back-end here, so the drop-down next to Internal Audio Player has a single entry. There is no FFmpeg player; see DEPENDENCIES.md.

To use a program of your own instead: Edit → Preferences → Audio, select External Audio Player and type its command line.

Note: The player command must be either in your system PATH or specified with an absolute path.

Linux/macOS examples:

vlc: 

vlc --intf dummy --play-and-exit --no-video

ffplay: 

ffplay -autoexit -nodisp

mpv: 

mpv --no-video --no-audio-display --no-config

or other audio player.

docs.title: Favorites
docs.text:
Favorites is a hierarchical structure of folders and words in them. You could create folders manually via context menu.

By default, the ⭐ icon on the toolbar will indiciate if word is in top most level.

You can "activate" a folder via context menu. Then the ⭐ icon will indiciate if a word is in this folder and clicking the ⭐ icon will add/remove words to/from this folder.

A group can have a associated folder. When switching groups, the associated folder will be automatically activated. For simple use cases, just use the name of an existing folder. If a folder is nested, then use / as a separator, such as english/food/spicy or spanish/greetings.

The entries can be moved simply by dragging and dropping. The entries can be deleted via context menu or by pressing the "Delete" key.

docs.title: Import & Export
docs.text:
In addition to adding and removing items to/from the Favorites you can perform the following operations via context menu or the main menu:

  • "Export" - Export the all favoriates to a plain text or XML file.
  • "Import" - The current favorites will be replaced by the content of XML or plain text.

Info

Currently, XML will perserve folder structure but plain text won't!

docs.title: Full-text search
docs.text:
Note

The dictionary indexes for full-text search in the background, started immediately after the program starts; the name of the dictionary being indexed is shown in the status line. This can take a long time and needs real resources. Turn indexing off per dictionary in preferences for the huge ones. To find out which dictionary cannot be indexed, run MicroDict with --log-to-file or watch stdout.

These full-text indexes can also take up a large amount of disk space. If the indexes fill up your system drive, you can move the index folder to another place using symbolic/hard links (see Move the index folder) or relocate all configurations and indexes by enabling Portable Mode.

The full-text search dialog can be opened via menu "Search" or "Ctrl+Shift+F".

Full-text search allow to search words or sentences not in dictionary headwords but in articles text of dictionaries from current dictionaries group.

Type the desired word in "Search line" to search.

Search modes

  • "Default" — This follows the xapian search syntax.
  • "Wildcards" - xpaian "wildcard" mode, which means it only supports the prefix wildcards like "hell*"(in English alike language).As CJK use NGRAM term generator,the * should be treated as a seperator while not quoted.

"Available dictionaries in group" - here you can view how many dictionaries in the current group are suitable for full-text search, how many dictionaries already indexed and how many dictionaries wait for indexing.

When you place mouse cursor over headword in results list, the tooltip with dictionary list contains such articles matched the search conditions will be shown.

docs.title: Headwords dialog
docs.text:
View the unique headwords list for local dictionary.

The headwords dialog can be opened via:

  • context menu of dictionaries list
  • context menu of icon on dictionaries bar in MicroDict toolbar
  • context menu of dictionaries list in navigation pane

The filter line allow to filter dictionaries list to remain only necessary headwords. Such filtration can be completed in next modes:

Mode Filtration type Plain text Headword contains string from filter line. Wildcards Headword matched to Unix-like template from filter line. Such template can contain wildcard symbols ? (matches any one character), * (matches any characters number) or ranges of characters [...] To find characters ?, *, [ and ] it should be escaped by backslash - \?, \*, \[, \]. RegExp Headword matched to regular expression from filter line.

If option "Auto apply" is turned on any changes in filter line will be applied to headwords list immediately. Otherwise you should press "Apply" button to apply changes. If dictionary contains more than 150000 headwords the "Auto apply" option is disabled.

If option "Match case" is turned on the matches search will be completed in the case-sensitive mode, otherwise in case-insensitive mode.

The "Export" button allow to export the filtered headwords list to text file.

Press "Ctrl+N" shortcut if you want to switch focus to main MicroDict window. Press "Ctrl+D" to switch focus from main window to headwords dialog.

docs.title: Global (system-wide) hotkey
docs.text:
One hotkey works while the window is not focused. On Linux and BSD it is requested from the desktop through org.freedesktop.portal.GlobalShortcuts, so the desktop decides who finally gets the key combination and can refuse it:

Hotkey (default) Action F12 Show the main window, then look up the clipboard contents

It is configured in Preferences → Hotkeys, and it needs a running xdg-desktop-portal; without one it is simply not registered. Pressing it shows the main window, reads the clipboard and searches for what it finds — one action, one window. There is no separate show/hide hotkey and no separate lookup hotkey.

A hotkey written as two combinations separated by a comma is a two-step sequence: the desktop can only grab a single combination, so MicroDict asks for the first one and matches the second press itself — the action fires only when the combination is pressed twice within half a second. A hotkey written as a single combination fires on the first press.

The desktop grabs the first combination exclusively: no other application can use it while MicroDict runs. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+C is therefore not a usable default — it is copy in every program on the desktop.

docs.title: The desktop hands out the binding
docs.text:
The requested combination is only a request: the desktop stores the binding in its own settings and asks you to press the key to confirm it. On KDE those stored bindings live in ~/.config/kglobalshortcutsrc, under a group named after the application; System Settings → Shortcuts writes there too. A stored sequence is not overwritten from the outside, so an application that merely asks again for a shortcut id it already registered is ignored.

MicroDict therefore releases the registration it no longer needs — on KDE that is org.kde.kglobalaccel.Component's cleanUp, which drops the application's group from that file — when it quits, and before it asks for a different combination. That is what makes a changed key in Preferences take effect, and it also clears a grab left behind by a process that was killed.

docs.title: The key has to mean the same thing in every keyboard layout
docs.text:
A compositor matches a global shortcut against the layout that is active at the moment of the press. A letter's keysym differs between layouts, so a letter-based default only fires in the layout it was written for: on KDE a Win+C grab never fires while a Russian layout is active. This is a known KDE defect, reported as KDE bug 457776 and, for Wayland, KDE bug 453661.

Function keys, arrows and the like carry the same keysym in every layout, which is why the default sits on F12. If you choose a letter, expect it to work only in the layout you typed it in.

docs.title: Wayland: the clipboard goes to the focused window
docs.text: On Wayland a client receives clipboard data only while it holds focus, so a background application cannot read the clipboard at all. The hotkey therefore shows the main window first and reads the clipboard a moment later — the window has to be focused before the data offer arrives.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
Type your word in Search Box and press Enter to search word in the current selected group. You can also choose a variant from a matches list.

Holding Ctrl or Shift will display the translation result in a new tab.

docs.title: Wildcard matching
docs.text:
The search line can use wildcard or glob symbols for matching words.

Wildcard Description ? Matches any single character. * Matches zero or more of any characters. [abc] Matches one character given in the bracket. [a-c] Matches one character from the range given in the bracket. [!abc] Matches one character that is not given in the bracket. [!a-c] Matches one character that is not from the range given in the bracket. \ Escaping wildcard symbols, e.g. \? to search ?

Note

The wildcard symbol in the first character leads to scanning of every dictionary's every word and may take a long time.

More information about wildcard matching can be found in Wikipedia's glob article.

docs.title: Dictionary Bar
docs.text:
The dictionary bar shows dictionaries from the current group.

Click the icons to select/unselect them.

docs.title: Single Selection
docs.text:
++ctrl+"Click"++ will focus on a single dictionary.

If a dictionary is the only one selected, clicking it with ++ctrl++ will reselect all dictionaries.

docs.title: Temporary Selection
docs.text:
Temporarily capture the selection and restore it later.

  • Capture Selection <-- ++shift+"Click"++ any dictionary icons.
  • Restore Selection <-- Click the "Restore selection" in the right click context menu

Note

the "Found in dictionaries" panel can also use the above two special operations.

docs.title: Build from source
docs.text:
The workflow files under .github — Release-appimage.yml for the release build, PR-check-cmake.yml for the dynamic ones — carry the actual build commands and are the reference.

The Linux release build is the fully static one; if that is all you want, ./build-appimage.sh at the repository root runs it in Docker and leaves build-out/MicroDict-<version>-<arch>.AppImage behind. See Build the static Linux binary — this page is for a normal dynamic build, which is what you want while developing.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• A C++23 compiler (GCC 13+ or Clang 17+; the static image uses GCC 15.2)
  • Qt 6 (6.8 or newer recommended; the fork's static build uses 6.12) — qtbase, qtsvg, qt5compat, qtmultimedia, qttools (for lrelease), and on Linux the Wayland platform plugin
  • The libraries MicroDict links (see DEPENDENCIES.md for why each one is there):
  • hunspell — spell checking
  • xapian — full-text index. Must be the 1.4 series: Alpine 3.24 and recent Debian/Ubuntu ship Xapian 2.0, whose C++ API this program does not target
  • OpenCC — Chinese conversion
  • toml++
  • FFmpeg and/or Qt Multimedia — audio playback
  • libvorbis, libogg — Vorbis in DSL sound archives
  • zlib, lzo2, xz (lzma) — compressed dictionary bodies. Not bzip2: it is not linked, and the image builds freetype without it so nothing else pulls it in either.
  • PulseAudio (libpulse) and D-Bus — audio output and the desktop portal
  • wayland client — global hotkeys go through the desktop portal, which is a Wayland/D-Bus service

docs.title: Alpine (the distribution this fork's build is defined against)
docs.text:
apk add build-base cmake ninja pkgconf python3 git \
    qt6-qtbase-dev qt6-qtsvg-dev qt6-qt5compat-dev qt6-qtmultimedia-dev \
    qt6-qttools-dev qt6-qtwayland-dev \
    hunspell-dev opencc-dev tomlplusplus-dev lzo-dev \
    xapian-core-dev ffmpeg-dev libpulse-dev dbus-dev wayland-dev \
    libvorbis-dev libogg-dev zlib-dev lzo-dev xz-dev \
    libxkbcommon-dev freetype-dev fontconfig-dev libpng-dev expat-dev \
    pcre2-dev libsndfile-dev gettext-dev fontconfig font-dejavu

Xapian is the exception: Alpine's xapian-core-dev is 2.0, so build xapian-core-1.4.x from source and point CMake at it, or use the Dockerfile, which does exactly that.

docs.title: Other distributions
docs.text:
The same set under different names. PR-check-cmake.yml builds against Debian/Ubuntu, Arch and macOS, so its three install lists are the exact package names:

  • Ubuntu 24.04: build-essential ninja-build libhunspell-dev libxapian-dev libopencc-dev liblzo2-dev libvorbis-dev zlib1g-dev libavutil-dev libavformat-dev libzstd-dev libxkbcommon-dev qt6-base-dev qt6-multimedia-dev qt6-tools-dev qt6-tools-dev-tools libtomlplusplus-dev
  • Arch: cmake ninja ffmpeg hunspell libvorbis lzo opencc qt6-base qt6-multimedia qt6-tools tomlplusplus xapian-core
  • macOS: brew install create-dmg ccache opencc ffmpeg@6 libao libiconv lzip libvorbis hunspell xapian tomlplusplus qt

None of them installs qt6-webengine-dev, qt6-webchannel-dev, qt6-speech-dev, libeb16-dev, libzim-dev, libxtst-dev or x11proto-record-dev — those were upstream's, for the features this fork does not have.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
cd MicroDict && mkdir build_dir
# config step
cmake -S . -B build_dir \
      -G Ninja \
      -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release

# actual build
cmake --build build_dir --parallel 7

The executable is microdict, and on Linux that is the end of it: there is no install step, because the program finds its read-only data relative to its own executable (Config::getProgramDataDir()), and its translations are linked into the executable itself. macOS does have a cmake --install step, because there the install tree is the deliverable.

docs.title: Feature flags
docs.text:
Append -D<flag>=ON/OFF to the config step:

Flag Default Meaning MICRODICT_STATIC_BUILD OFF Link everything from .a archives: no NEEDED, no PT_INTERP. Needs a toolchain with static libc/libstdc++ (Alpine) and a Qt built with BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF. See cmake/Deps_Linux.cmake for the archive list and the --undefined= tricks static linking forces WITH_QT_MULTIMEDIA ON Qt Multimedia — the only internal audio player. It also pulls in the FFmpeg libraries, because Qt's own media plugin decodes through them and a static build links that plugin in.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Built from an IDE, the produced MicroDict.app runs from the IDE, which sets up the paths for you.

cmake --install build_dir/ runs macdeployqt, ad-hoc code signing and the rest; the app bundle ends up in build_dir/redist/MicroDict.app. To also produce a .dmg, install create-dmg first.

docs.title: Build the static Linux binary
docs.text:
The Linux release of MicroDict is one file with no shared-library dependencies: 0 NEEDED entries, no PT_INTERP, no bundled fonts. It runs on any x86-64 or aarch64 Linux — glibc or musl, any distribution, any version — that has a Wayland compositor. Shipped as an AppImage, which is that binary plus its translations, icon and desktop entry: one file per architecture.

The recipe is packaging/docker/Dockerfile. Docker is only the build farm: the results are copied out of the image, and the image itself is not needed to run the program.

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
cd MicroDict
./build-appimage.sh              # the AppImage only, into build-out/
./packaging/docker/build.sh      # the whole image, plus the bare binary

build.sh builds the image, runs the checks inside it, and extracts:

build-out/microdict                    # the binary, translations linked into it
build-out/MicroDict-<version>-<arch>.AppImage
build-out/portalmock                   # the portal test double, see below

From scratch this compiles Qt and every dependency, so expect roughly half an hour on 32 cores. Later runs reuse Docker's layer cache; changing only the program's own sources re-runs just the last steps.

The image is architecture-neutral: TARGETARCH picks the matching AppImage runtime and names the output MicroDict-<version>-x86_64.AppImage or MicroDict-<version>-aarch64.AppImage. Build each one natively — docker buildx build --platform linux/arm64 on an arm64 host — because the same build under QEMU emulation is 5–20× slower, which is what the release workflow does not have to pay for.

To build without extracting:

docker build -f packaging/docker/Dockerfile -t microdict-static .

to stop after the dependencies (Qt + everything else) are built:

docker build -f packaging/docker/Dockerfile --target deps -t microdict-deps .

and to rebuild only the AppImage stage:

docker build -f packaging/docker/Dockerfile --target appimage -t microdict-appimage .

docs.title: Why it has to be Alpine
docs.text:
musl is the only libc that is sane to link statically; glibc's static libc pulls in NSS and dlopen stubs and refuses to do DNS or locale lookups without a matching runtime. Everything therefore comes from Alpine 3.24, and everything Alpine does not ship as a .a archive is built from source in the image: Qt 6.12 (qtbase, qtsvg, qtwayland, qtmultimedia, qtshadertools, qttools), GNU libiconv, wayland, libffi, hunspell, xapian-core 1.4, OpenCC, LZO, toml++, FFmpeg, PulseAudio and D-Bus. Each download is pinned by sha256. The version choices and the reasons are in DEPENDENCIES.md.

Two consequences worth knowing:

  • Qt plugins are compiled in. A static binary cannot dlopen() a plugin, so the platform plugin (wayland, offscreen), the image formats, the multimedia backend and the xdgdesktopportal platform theme are imported at link time by qt_import_plugins() in CMakeLists.txt.
  • The host tools Qt builds must be static too. With dynamic host tools, musl's static-TLS surplus makes the TLS offsets baked into libQt6Core.a wrong and every tool dies inside QThread::currentThread() — rcc --help segfaults. That is why CMAKE_EXE_LINKER_FLAGS=-static is passed to the Qt builds.

docs.title: The AppImage
docs.text:
packaging/docker/appimage.sh wraps the binary in the last stage of the image. It is the only Linux packaging the fork does — there are no install() rules, no CPack generators, no Flatpak and no AppStream metadata anywhere in the tree.

An AppImage is a squashfs of a program tree with a small runtime prepended to it, and the format is three commands:

size=$(stat -c %s runtime-x86_64)
mksquashfs AppDir out.AppImage -offset "$size" -comp zstd -b 1048576 \
           -root-owned -noappend -mkfs-time 0
dd if=runtime-x86_64 of=out.AppImage conv=notrunc bs=65536
chmod 755 out.AppImage

-offset is what makes it work: mksquashfs leaves size bytes of padding at the front and computes every internal offset as if the image started there, and the runtime then overwrites exactly that padding. The runtime finds its payload as "the squashfs that begins where this ELF ends", so there is no table of contents to patch and nothing to sign — the type-2 runtime reads only the .upd_info and .sha256_sig ELF sections, and neither is required.

Notes that cost some experimenting:

  • appimagetool is not used. It is a glibc program and this image is musl. Its recipe is the three commands above, and the runtime it would embed is pinned by sha256 instead — 20251108 from AppImage/type2-runtime, a static musl binary, one per architecture (runtime-x86_64, runtime-aarch64), which is also why the AppImage can be run as a check inside the build.
  • Compression is zstd, not xz. That runtime's bundled squashfuse was built with zlib and zstd only; asking it for xz fails with "Squashfs image uses xz compression, this version supports only zlib, zstd".
  • The AppDir mirrors an FHS tree (usr/bin next to usr/share/microdict/) because that is what the program expects: Config::getProgramDataDir() is resolved relative to the executable, not compiled in from $PREFIX.
  • OpenCC's data travels. libopencc.a has /usr/share/opencc compiled into it, and inside a mounted AppImage that path is the host's, not the bundle's. So the .json/.ocd2 files go into the program's own data dir and Config::getOpenCCDir() names that directory when it exists.

docs.title: The checks that run inside the image
docs.text:
The build fails unless all five pass — qtprobe.sh, portalmock.sh, smoke.sh, migtest.sh and appimage.sh. What each of those files is and what it proves: packaging/docker/README.md.

Then the image asserts the link is really static — ! ldd is not a valid test on this stack, because musl's ldd exits 0 for a static-pie image:

file build/microdict            # says "static-pie linked"
[ "$(readelf -l build/microdict | grep -c INTERP)" = 0 ]
! readelf -d build/microdict | grep -qE 'NEEDED|RPATH|RUNPATH'

portalmock is also copied out to build-out/portalmock, so the same desktop double can be driven against the extracted binary on the host:

build-out/portalmock --serve-theme 40     # dark -> light -> dark, printing each step

docs.title: What those checks do not cover
docs.text:
None of the five scripts ever opens a Babylon .bgl: mkdict.py generates a StarDict dictionary and smoke.sh loads an xdxf folder, so Babylon::readBlock() and the readEntry() loop that builds a .bgl index have no automated test. Checking them needs a real .bgl, and those cannot be shipped here — they are Babylon's own files. One that is freely downloadable and does the job:

https://archive.org/download/BabylonEnglishSpanish/Babylon_English_Spanish.BGL
sha256 38791c9d8f63cdc3622052f2df31ddced9d0b37c8814bf09bf856b8727c02d32   7 225 214 B

Put it in a folder, point a <paths><path> entry at it, and start the program. The log should show Bgl: Building the index for dictionary: …, then Default charset: WINDOWS-1252, Writing index…, Building a tree of 493 elements, Load done; a lookup of house then comes back from Babylon English-Spanish. That file carries 161 879 headwords, 231 839 alternate spellings and 2 resource records, so it drives the block loop hard — which is where the buffer ownership lives.

docs.title: Running the result
docs.text:
./build-out/MicroDict-<version>-<arch>.AppImage <word>   # or chmod +x and double-click
./build-out/microdict <word>                             # the bare binary

Either way it uses the host's fonts (/etc/fonts), the host's desktop portal for hotkeys and colours, and its own configuration folders — see Configuration folders.

If you run the image instead of the extracted files, the container decides which fonts exist; mount the host's if you want the same text as everywhere else:

docker run --rm -e XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/cfg -v $PWD/cfg:/cfg -v $PWD/dicts:/dicts \
    -v /usr/share/fonts:/usr/share/fonts:ro --device /dev/shm microdict-static <word>

docs.title: Add a program as a dictionary
Add external programs or scripts
docs.text: MicroDict can use programs or scripts as dictionary.

docs.title: An example
docs.text: Tokenize the input german sentence into words.

docs.title: Install Python and SoMaJo.
docs.text:
You can follow the instructions in the documentation https://github.com/tsproisl/SoMaJo?tab=readme-ov-file#installation

pip install -U SoMaJo

docs.title: Create a script
docs.text:
from somajo import SoMaJo
import sys

tokenizer = SoMaJo("de_CMC", split_camel_case=True)

# note that paragraphs are allowed to contain newlines
paragraphs = [sys.argv[1]]
sentences = tokenizer.tokenize_text(paragraphs)
for sentence in sentences:
    for token in sentence:
        if token.token_class=='regular':
            print(f"{token.text}")

and save the script as ~/dictscripts/somajo.py, made executable.

docs.title: Add the script to the program dictionary
docs.text: python3 ~/dictscripts/somajo.py %GDWORD%

docs.title: How to customize OpenCC
docs.text:
Under the opencc folder are the OpenCC configuration files.

Where that folder is depends on how the program was delivered: inside an AppImage it is usr/share/microdict/opencc/ in the image (mounted read-only), in a macOS bundle it is an opencc/ folder next to the executable, and in a dynamic build against a distro's OpenCC there is no such folder at all — the library's own compiled-in /usr/share/opencc is used. Config::getOpenCCDir() is what decides, and it names a bundled directory only when that directory exists.

The Chinese and Japanese character conversion uses the following files:

File Conversion s2tw.json Simplified Chinese to Traditional Chinese (Taiwan standard) s2hk.json Simplified Chinese to Traditional Chinese (Hong Kong variant) t2s.json Traditional Chinese to Simplified Chinese s2t.json Simplified Chinese to Traditional Chinese, the first step of the Japanese conversion t2jp.json Traditional Chinese (Kyūjitai) to Japanese Shinjitai jp2t.json Japanese Shinjitai to Traditional Chinese (Kyūjitai)

jp2t.json is used as an extra normalization step in front of the Chinese conversions, so Japanese Shinjitai input can also match the Chinese entries. It is applied as a separate conversion chain whose results are merged with the plain one; therefore, it can only add candidates and never replace a plain conversion result.

docs.text:

1. Find out the index filename of the dictionary: You can find the index filename by right clicking on the dictionary in the dictionary bar.
