docs.title: Update the Crowdin .ts file
docs.text: This project uses Crowdin to organize its translations. When new translatable strings appear in the sources, locale/crowdin.ts has to be refreshed: that file is what Crowdin shows the translators, and the per-language .ts files come back from it.

docs.title: How to update the crowdin.ts file
docs.text:
lupdate -no-obsolete -no-ui-lines -locations none src -ts locale/crowdin.ts

lupdate ships with Qt Tools — qt6-tools-dev on Debian/Ubuntu, qt6-qttools-dev on Alpine, qt6-tools on Arch.

the option -no-obsolete will remove obsolete items from crowdin.ts file.

the option -no-ui-lines will not generate line numbers in the crowdin.ts file. The line numbers change too often, which will make too many code changes between commits.

The Crowdin side of it is configured by crowdin.yml in the repository root.

docs.title: How OCR reaches the program
docs.text:
Any OCR program supporting "post-capture actions" can integrate seamlessly with MicroDict.

A few examples are provided below, though many similar tools are available.

docs.title: Clipboard Hotkey Mode
docs.text:
This is the universal method: it works with any OCR program that can copy its recognition result to the system clipboard.

  1. Configure your OCR program to copy the recognized text to the clipboard after recognition — Capture2Text, OCRSpace, ScreenTranslate and most others can do this.
  2. Press MicroDict's global hotkey (F12 by default). The main window opens and the clipboard contents are searched.

On Wayland the clipboard is readable only by the focused window, which is why the hotkey opens the window first and reads the clipboard immediately afterwards.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Works with any OCR tool that can write to the clipboard
  • No command-line arguments or executable paths to configure

docs.title: Capture2Text
docs.text:
Capture2Text can call executable after capturing, and you can set the executable to MicroDict.

Detailed usage document: Capture2Text

Capture2Text Download

For example, change the Output action Call Executable to the program you run:

/usr/local/bin/microdict "${capture}"

The full path of an AppImage works just as well — it is an executable file, so it can be the command.

Then press Win+Q and select a region. After capturing a word, Capture2Text forwards it to the running MicroDict, which looks it up in its main window.

The hotkeys can be configured.

Capture2Text can also obtain word near the cursor without selecting a region via the "Forward Text Line Capture" by pressing Win+W

you may want to enable "First word only" so that only a single word would be captured

docs.title: Use Capture2Text on Linux
docs.text: Capture2Text does not have a Linux version, but I have ported it to Linux https://github.com/xiaoyifang/Capture2Text thanks to Capture2Text Linux Port and to sikmir, who reported the upstream build problem.

docs.title: Tesseract via command line
docs.text:
On Linux, you can combine command line screenshot then pass the output image to Tesseract then pass the text result to microdict

Example with spectacle (KDE) and grim (wayland/wlroots)

#!/usr/bin/env bash

set -e

case $DESKTOP_SESSION in
    sway)
        grim -g "$(slurp)" /tmp/tmp.just_random_name.png
    ;;
    plasmawayland | plasma)
        spectacle --region --nonotify --background \
        --output /tmp/tmp.just_random_name.png
    ;;
    *)
        echo "Failed to know desktop type"
        exit 1
    ;;
esac

# note that tesseract will apppend .txt to output file
tesseract /tmp/tmp.just_random_name.png /tmp/tmp.just_random_name --oem 1  -l eng

microdict "$(cat /tmp/tmp.just_random_name.txt)"

rm /tmp/tmp.just_random_name.png
rm /tmp/tmp.just_random_name.txt

docs.title: Step 1: Install Required Software (Dependencies)
docs.text:
Depending on your system, you need to install the following tools:

  • OCR Engine: tesseract and its language packs.
  • Screenshot Tool: Choose according to your desktop environment:
    • KDE (Plasma): Install spectacle.
    • Sway (Wayland): Install grim and slurp.
  • Other: bash environment.

Example installation for Ubuntu/Debian:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install tesseract-ocr tesseract-ocr-eng tesseract-ocr-chi-sim  spectacle

Note: chi-sim is the Chinese language pack. The script example only uses English eng, but it's recommended to include Chinese as well.

docs.title: Step 2: Create the Script File
docs.text:
Create a new file in your home directory, for example ocr_translate.sh:

nano ~/ocr_translate.sh

Copy the code above into it (or type it manually).

Save and exit (In Nano, press Ctrl+O, then Enter, then Ctrl+X).

docs.title: Step 3: Make It Executable
docs.text:
Run the following command in terminal to make the script executable:

chmod +x ~/ocr_translate.sh

docs.title: Step 4: Use the Script
docs.text:
1. Start MicroDict first (let it run in the background).
  2. Execute the script:
./ocr_translate.sh

Operation:

If you're using KDE, your mouse will turn into a crosshair. Drag to select the text region you want to translate. The script will automatically recognize the text, and the running MicroDict will look it up in its main window.

docs.title: Set Up a Keyboard Shortcut
docs.text: This is the most recommended way to use it. In your system settings -> Shortcuts, add a global shortcut (such as Ctrl + Alt + G) pointing to the absolute path of this script (e.g., /home/your_username/ocr_translate.sh). This way, whenever you see an unknown word, just press the shortcut to capture it.

docs.title: Support Chinese Recognition
docs.text:
If you need to recognize Chinese, modify the tesseract line in the script:

Change -l eng to -l eng+chi_sim (requires the Chinese language pack to be installed).

docs.title: For GNOME Users
docs.text:
If you're using GNOME desktop, the case in the script won't match. You can add a GNOME screenshot command, or use the more generic:

gnome-screenshot -a -f /tmp/tmp.just_random_name.png
